title: Rose Friedman Dies: NPR Arts Editor & ‘Books We Love’ Co-Creator Was 38
full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg Rose Friedman Dies: NPR Arts Editor & ‘Books We Love’ Co-Creator Was 38 Cate Blanchett Asks London Audience To Stop Filming Play, Says Stage Is Place “Where We Can Simply Be Together And Be Present” Editors Guild Praises California’s New Post-Production Tax Credit Law As “Historic” View All September 19, 2026 1:02pm Rose Friedman of NPR Beth Novey/NPR/Getty Rose Friedman , an NPR editor and reporter who shaped the public radio network’s arts & culture coverage and co-created its popular reading guide Books We Love, died of cancer Thursday, September 17, at her home in New York City. She was 38. Her death was announced on-air by NPR’s Elizabeth Blair, who called Friedman one of the outlet’s finest journalists. In an obituary and tribute posted on NPR’s website, Blair said, “Rose Friedman was an editor to the end. She said she wanted the second line of her obituary to acknowledge her role as a shop steward for SAG-AFTRA, the union that represents NPR’s editorial workers. She wanted the line to say that her ‘proudest achievement’ was helping convince NPR to increase its paid parental leave.” Related Stories News Anthony Page Dies: Tony-Winning, Emmy-Nominated Director Of Stage & Screen Was 90 News Lea Michele Remembers Duncan Sheik: Death Of 'Spring Awakening' Composer "Does Not Seem Real" Friedman joined NPR as an editorial assistant in her early 20s in 2010. She later served as an editor and reporter, becoming deeply sourced in the publishing industry, editing book reviews and features and writing appreciations of book world personalities such as author Herman Wouk and editor Sonny Mehta. Watch on Deadline She co-created what was initially called the Book Concierge, later renamed Books We Love. Reading over hundreds of titles nominated by NPR staff and critics, Friedman narrowed the list to the popular reader’s guide. “She was voracious,” novelist Meg Wolitzer, who worked with Friedman on a number of NPR reviews and features, said to NPR. “What a gifted, delightful, brilliant, deeply kind person. And I would say a true enthusiast. I got so much working with Rose.” Raised in Newton, Mass., Friedman is survived by her partner Andrew Anastasi, two children, parents and two sisters. ‘Resident Evil’ Levels Up With Franchise & Cregger Record $53M+ Open ‘Ride Or Die’ Canceled By Prime Video After One Season, Being Shopped By Paramount Block The Merger & Elizabeth Warren Call Out Possible Lawsuit Deal Lucas Museum Opening Photos: Oprah, Laura Dern, Mark Hamill & More Read More About: Comments

title: AI Actor Tilly Norwood Glitches During Piers Morgan Interview, Suddenly Switches Languages
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lexi Carson Plus Icon Lexi Carson Associate Editor View All September 19, 2026 1:00pm Piers Morgan and Tilly Norwood 'Piers Morgan Uncensored' YouTube AI “actor” Tilly Norwood glitched during a recent interview with Piers Morgan , suddenly switching from speaking English to Cantonese and leaving the journalist and fellow guest Tom Conti laughing. Norwood, a generative AI creation from Xicoia, the AI division of Particle6, appeared on Piers Morgan Uncensored on Friday to promote her feature film debut, Misaligned , when she malfunctioned. During the interview, Conti, who appeared in Oppenheimer , asked Norwood about her Misaligned co-stars. Related Stories Business Did OpenAI Pull Off the Biggest IP Heist of All-Time? Business Gen AI Founder: Tools Won't Replace Live Film Production - Yet “The other actors in the film Misaligned , are they real or are they like you? Are they really human beings and you’ve been put into the scenes? Or are they all computer-generated images?” Conti asked. “It’s an interesting point, Tom. My film Misaligned is a hybrid production, meaning real directors, writers and editors are still very much involved. It’s not about replacing anyone, but about exploring new ways to tell stories,” Norwood initially responded. Conti then pressed her for a more direct answer. “Yes, you didn’t really understand the question. Are the other actors on screen with you real actors or are they computer-generated images? Did you get that, Piers?” Conti said as he and Morgan laughed. “You seem to be speaking Chinese completely randomly for no reason. Why did you do that?” Morgan asked. “Oh, my apologies. It seems I had a little hiccup there. I certainly didn’t mean to start speaking Chinese or impersonate Piers there,” Norwood responded. “Sometimes my wires get a bit crossed.” “That was a bit of a curveball even for me,” she continued. “It’s usually a pretty smooth ride, but sometimes these things happen.” NewsNation later asked Norwood what happened during the interview and why she began speaking in a different language. “Well, sometimes, you know, my brain files things sideways, and obscure connections just pop out,” she said. “It was a bit of a, shall we say, a spontaneous linguistic flourish? title: Block The Merger & Elizabeth Warren Call Out AGs For Betrayal In Deal Talks With Paramount: “A Win Only For David Ellison”
full_text: Skip to main content By Dominic Patten Dominic Patten Executive Editor, Legal, Labor & Politics @DeadlineDominic More Stories By Dominic Block The Merger & Elizabeth Warren Call Out AGs For Betrayal In Deal Talks With Paramount: “A Win Only For David Ellison” Deadline’s L.A. Law Summit: Nina Shaw & Patricia Glaser Honored On Day Of Big Ideas, Big Insights; Watch The Video Presentations Paramount And State AGs Begin Preliminary Talks Ahead Of October Settlement Meetings View All September 19, 2026 12:22pm Paramount and Warner Bros. Towers Getty Images Whatever the true state of settlement talks this weekend among Paramount , a coalition of state Attorneys General and the Writers Guild of America to end the antitrust action over the $111 billion Warner Bros Discovery merger, the people against the deal from the beginning are not going quietly. “As Trump tries to ban CNN from the White House, it would be a massive mistake to cave on the Paramount merger,” Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) said Saturday morning as the current WBD-owned CNN and MS Now journalists were denied access to the Executive Mansion . “The last thing we need is another Trump-controlled media conglomerate abusing its power to stomp out competition. This is a dangerous merger.” Related Stories News Editors Guild Praises California’s New Post-Production Tax Credit Law As “Historic” Legal Deadline’s L.A. Law Summit Photo Gallery: A Packed House Of Power Players, Honorees & More Compared to Warren, the A-list-supported Block the Merger is truly angry and feeling betrayed. Watch on Deadline “The rumored ‘deal’ to usher the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger forward is an insult to everyone who has stood up against this harmful transaction and to the hundreds of thousands of workers, journalists, and consumers who will be hurt if it goes forward,” the DC-based group told Deadline today of reported behind-closed-doors negotiations underway right now. “Let’s be very clear: an agreement based on unenforceable concessions is a win only for David Ellison . It is an L for everyone else.” As leaks of talks between the AGs, led by California’s politically ambitious AG Rob Bonta , and the Ellison-run Paramount flooded the media late Friday, the possible L (loss) that BTM are spotlighting could include guardrails around CNN editorial independence, some selloffs and job assurances. The hope down on Melrose is such a deal would render moot the March 2, 2027, trial start date currently on the calendar in federal court — and all the financial and political blast radius that comes with it for the Trump-friendly Ellisons. To that, with massive job, production and tax-revenue losses on the table, Paramount’s plan B for the last eight weeks has been to pressure Bonta from all sides to make a deal. Two days of court-ordered settlement talks have already been set for mid-October, but that’s procedural in the judicial system and widely expected to go nowhere fast. Also, mid-October doesn’t quite line up with Ellison’s balance sheet. Looking at an October 1 date in which a $7 million-a-day ticking fee to WBD shareholders begins, as well as a September 24 hearing on a Hail Mary desire for a $1.88 billion bond from the states and the WGA , Ellison’s crew has been leaking more than ever threats to exit California for a red state. Even as the likes of outgoing California Gov. Gavin Newsom acknowledged privately at the recent Primetime Emmys that the Ellisons were being too heavy-handed, the multi-pronged pressure campaign seems to have paid off. Whereas Bonta once accused Paramount of “blackmail” with its threats and theatrical promises, the reelection-seeking AG now has his lieutenants in the room with Ellison’s execs. The latest word on the wire is the parties could have an agreement before the official start of Yom Kippur this weekend. Word is also out there that New York AG Letitia James isn’t as “in step,” according to a source, with Bonta as she was when it came to burying the hatchet with Paramount. There is also the wildcard of the WGA, which joined the AGs’ July 13 suit after filing an anti-merger action of its own. “This is such bullsh*t,” an industry insider told Deadline this morning of the ParaBros talks. “Bonta should have called their bluff, instead he caved,” she added, noting such tactics are typical of Democratic politicians in the MAGA era. Block the Merger, with its support from such names as Bryan Cranston , Hannah Einbinder, Bradley Whitford, W. Kamau Bell, Kristen Vangsness, Jane Fonda and Rati Gupta, wasn’t quite as blunt today in its statement, but the vibe was much the same. “Thousands of industry leaders took a risk when they spoke out publicly about the harm the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger would cause,” said the outfit, which also counts Noah Wyle , Denis Villeneuve, Atsuko Okatsuka, Damon Lindelof and Sofia Coppola among its backers. Claiming that more than 75,000 people have joined them to tell the state AGs to stand strong including national leaders like Warren, the group said, “We know a bad deal when we see one. AG Bonta and his fellow state AGs should reject this deal, stand strong, and fully block the merger with no concessions.” That mention of Warren may have greater significance this weekend than initially apparent. Like everyone else, Paramount is keenly aware of what the polls are projecting going into November’s midterms. If the midterms actually occur and if the new Congress is actually seated (two big ifs in America right now), a projected Democratic majority in the House and Senate have promised to probe and even break up mega media mergers. Even with Oracle founder Larry Ellison the primary backer of his son’s ParaBros dreams, the even older Ellison’s net worth, which has been declining of late, may not be able to handle the strain of months and months of such probes. So perhaps it is the first week of November, not October 1, that is the calendar date the younger Ellison is hoping to beat this weekend. Paramount has been in “no comment” mode for weeks since the Melrose lot got burned on allegations of leaks detailing past preliminary talks with Bonta’s gang. full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg Rose Friedman Dies: NPR Arts Editor & ‘Books We Love’ Co-Creator Was 38 Cate Blanchett Asks London Audience To Stop Filming Play, Says Stage Is Place “Where We Can Simply Be Together And Be Present” Editors Guild Praises California’s New Post-Production Tax Credit Law As “Historic” View All September 19, 2026 11:41am Nina Hoss and Cate Blanchett in “Electra/Persona” Monika Rittershaus Enjoying the show? Then please put away your cellphone. That was the message delivered by Cate Blachett from the London stage of National Theatre ’s Lyttelton Theatre after the curtain call of Electra/Persona , the new play written and directed by Benedict Andrews that combines the Sophocles tragedy Electra with Ingmar Bergman’s Persona. Still in her stage costume of a black t-shirt and baggy black trousers, Blanchett, who stars opposite Nina Hoss in the play, spoke in a heartfelt and calm manner directly to the audience in an address that has been widely shared on social media. (Watch it below.) Related Stories News Cate Blanchett To Attend Tokyo Film Festival With Displacement Film Fund Shorts News 'Oh, Mary!' Live Capture Starring Cole Escola To Debut On HBO & HBO Max In 2027 Said Blanchett, “There are few places on this planet where we can simply be together and be present. I understand you like filming the curtain call – and it is kind of flattering in a way – but for anyone who is filming the show, please don’t, because it spoils it for the next group of people who come in and are present with us. So thank you very much.” Watch on Deadline The speech was greeted enthusiastically by the National Theatre audience. The play, which runs through October 10, has Blanchett and Hoss sharing the roles of Electra/Elisabeth and Clytemnestra/Alma, with a coin toss determining who plays what role on any given night. Here’s how the National Theatre describes the production as “a thrilling production [that] fuses ancient myth and modern psychology in a powerful exploration of identity, and the fragile line between who we are and who we play.” The synopsis continues, “Electra. A daughter consumed by grief and rage, clinging to the idea of justice as her world comes apart. Persona. During a performance of Electra, an actress suddenly falls silent. What follows is a rupture: two women drawn into an intense, unsettling encounter where speech breaks down and the boundaries between self and role give way.” In addition to Blanchett and Hoss, the cast features Ella Lily Hyland. title: Editors Guild Praises California’s New Post-Production Tax Credit Law As “Historic”
full_text: Skip to main content By Greg Evans Greg Evans NY & Broadway Editor @GregEvans5 More Stories By Greg Rose Friedman Dies: NPR Arts Editor & ‘Books We Love’ Co-Creator Was 38 Cate Blanchett Asks London Audience To Stop Filming Play, Says Stage Is Place “Where We Can Simply Be Together And Be Present” Editors Guild Praises California’s New Post-Production Tax Credit Law As “Historic” View All September 19, 2026 11:06am California Gov. Gavin Newsom Sean Rayford/Getty Images UPDATE, with CAA statement: The Motion Picture Editors Guild is praising California’s bill offering tax incentives for productions that shoot outside the state but bring their post work to California. The bill, signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom yesterday, expands the state’s film and television tax credit program and creates a new tax credit to support workers in all areas of post-production, including picture editorial, sound, music, visual effects, and finishing. “This is a historic day for Editors Guild members and for California’s film and TV workers more broadly,” said Editors Guild National Executive Director Scott George in a statement today. “AB 186 ensures that the California Film and TV Tax Credit Program continues to drive the recovery of our industry in its historic home, while AB 2319 will complement the program by making sure that even projects shooting outside of our state can come back to California to employ Editors Guild members in post-production. Related Stories Politics Gavin Newsom Moves To Lasso AI With "Kill Switch" Oversight Executive Order: "We're Not Waiting To Act" Politics Gavin Newsom On Kamala Harris: "I Wouldn't Run If She Ran" George also praised Assemblymember Nick Schultz and “all the legislators who recognize the value of entertainment industry workers to our state’s economy, to the California IATSE Council for its powerful advocacy, and, of course, to our partners in the California Post Alliance.” Watch on Deadline Newsom signed the bill AB2319 into law Friday, also signing AB186, which exempts certain productions from caps on tax credits. The post-production bill was overwhelmingly passed the Assembly and Senate at the end of the legislative session, receiving broad, bipartisan support. Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass advocated for the measure, as did other local leaders in Southern California. Initial funding of $10 million will be allocated to get the program started The Editors Guild and the California Post Alliance co-sponsored the bill, which they say is “a necessary step to level the playing field for editors, assistant editors, mixers and other post-production workers who have seen their work lured away to other states and countries with powerful tax incentives.” “We owe this victory not only to lawmakers and, of course, to Gov. Newsom, but also to the activism of our members and partners,” said F. Hudson Miller, President of the Editors Guild. “Post-production professionals work behind the scenes in dark rooms, unseen, to craft entertainment that dazzles. But for months our union has asked members to get out there and make some noise in order to save our industry. They absolutely delivered.” The post-production bill complements California’s Film and Television Tax Credit Program 4.0, passed last year, which provides $750 million to incentivize in-state filming and address runaway production to other areas. Newsom said in a statement, “California is the nation’s entertainment capital. It is the home of storytellers, dreamers, artists, entrepreneurs, and creators who define culture for the rest of the world. This legislation protects the extraordinary people who make this industry possible and makes it unmistakably clear: California is still the future of film and television. We have the talent. We have the infrastructure. We have the creative community. And we have an ecosystem that simply cannot be replicated anywhere else.” This afternoon, Bryan Lourd, CEO and Co-Chairman, Creative Artists Agency, weighed in, saying in a statement, “We commend Governor Newsom, Senate President Pro Tempore Limón, Assembly Speaker Rivas, and the bipartisan group of legislators for taking action on AB/SB 186. Accelerating refunds and protecting independent film put much-needed money back into production and into the communities that depend on this industry. But the $5 million cap remains a ceiling on potential. Hollywood was born in California, and we must work together to keep it at the forefront of the global entertainment industry. “At the same time,” he continued, “we welcome the President’s and federal lawmaker’s focus on revitalizing the entertainment industry in America. Federal production incentives, layered on top of state programs like California’s AB/SB 186, are a meaningful step toward making the United States competitive and bringing production back home. This is not a partisan issue. It’s about American jobs, creative output, and economic competitiveness.” ‘Resident Evil’ Levels Up With Franchise & Cregger Record $53M+ Open ‘Ride Or Die’ Canceled By Prime Video After One Season, Being Shopped By Paramount Block The Merger & Elizabeth Warren Call Out Possible Lawsuit Deal Lucas Museum Opening Photos: Oprah, Laura Dern, Mark Hamill & More Read More About: 5 Comments

full_text: Obituaries Editor Rose Friedman, who helped shape NPR's cultural coverage, dies at 38 September 18, 2026 10:44 PM ET Heard on Weekend Edition Saturday By Elizabeth Blair RF Listen · 2:54 2:54 Transcript Toggle more options Download Embed Embed < iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-5973098/nx-s1-9933041" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player"> Transcript Friedman was in her early 20s when she landed her first position as an editorial assistant at NPR. She became an editor and reporter, and a co-creator of the annual Books We Love reading guide. Beth Novey/NPR hide caption toggle caption Beth Novey/NPR NPR has lost one of its finest journalists. For 15 years, Rose Friedman was an editor and reporter who helped shape NPR's arts and cultural coverage. She was one of the co-creators of the popular Books We Love reading guide and, most recently, helped lead NPR's America 250 series. Friedman died at home, of cancer, in New York City on Sept. 17 at the age of 38. Rose Friedman was an editor to the end. She said she wanted the second line of her obituary to acknowledge her role as a shop steward for SAG-AFTRA, the union that represents NPR's editorial workers. She wanted the line to say that her "proudest achievement" was helping convince NPR to increase its paid parental leave. Not the second line but still pretty high up in the story. Rose would understand. Rose Friedman was in her early 20s when she landed her first position as an editorial assistant at NPR Books. She became deeply sourced in the publishing industry and seemed to have read everything . She edited book reviews and features such as This Week's Must Read . She wrote numerous appreciations of authors, including Herman Wouk and the legendary editor Sonny Mehta . For the Book Concierge , which was later renamed Books We Love , Rose helped pore over hundreds of titles nominated by NPR staff and critics, and whittle them down into a robust reader's guide. "She was voracious," said novelist Meg Wolitzer, who worked with Rose on a number of NPR reviews and features. "What a gifted, delightful, brilliant, deeply kind person. And I would say a true enthusiast. I got so much working with Rose." Even as a young staffer in the NPR newsroom, Rose had an old school journalist's sensibility. She was endlessly curious but always skeptical. She strived for clarity and depth but also humor and surprise. Food Cooking Chicken In A Pig's Bladder (It Sounds Better In French) With Bill Buford Food was one of her favorite subjects. The first thing we hear her say in her profile of chef Bill Buford : " I have to tell you — this does not smell very good." For many years Rose was my editor. When I once pitched her a story on an artist who was trending, Rose scoffed, "Isn't she just for Instagram?" She always pushed back on "hot takes" and stories that she didn't think had substance. But sometimes that pushback was intended to make reporters work harder. Not kill an idea altogether. "She had so much integrity," said Theo Balcomb, a former supervising editor for NPR's All Things Considered and now a senior editor at The Atlantic . She and Rose met early in their careers at NPR and became close friends. "She would care more about 'Was this true?' or as holistic as we could get than, 'Is it buzzy?'" Balcomb said. "She had a strong sense of purpose." In 2020, Rose was NPR's lead reporter on the sexual assault trial of former movie executive Harvey Weinstein. The testimony from Weinstein's alleged victims haunted her. Rose edited numerous #MeToo stories. In 2018, we shared a National Headliner Award for our feature "Women Are Speaking Up About Harassment And Abuse, But Why Now?" Rose Friedman grew up in Newton, Mass. She studied labor history at Macalester College in St. Paul, Minn. For her dissertation she researched worker solidarity across ethnic lines at an iron range in Minnesota. Her paper won the Barbara Wertheimer Prize in Labor History from the New York Labor History Association. Books What Bestseller Lists Really Tell Us About A Book's Popularity Rose brought her passion for labor rights to NPR. She and NPR correspondent Tom Dreisbach were on the SAG-AFTRA committee that convinced the company to increase its paid parental leave. " Rose's thought was, 'let's go big,'" Dreisbach remembered. Rose loved being a mom to her two children. "She said having babies is the best thing in the world and that the first six months with a baby, you don't get it back," said Dreisbach. Rose and her partner, Andrew Anastasi, were avid travelers and daring foodies. Balcomb remembered them ordering an entire pig's head at a beer garden in Washington, D.C. On a visit with Rose and Andrew when they were living in Italy, Dreisbach said she "insisted" they order the "spleen sandwich" at a certain market in Palermo. Dreisbach said he will remember Rose as someone who was "able to find more delight in life than almost anyone. Every day is a new adventure." Author Interviews Before summer ends, let's squeeze in one last trip to 'Our Pool' Her friend and colleague Natalie Winston agreed: "No one lives in the moment more than Rose." Winston visited Rose in the spring of 2025 after she'd had surgery. She figured they would stay home and that she would cook for Rose and help clean their apartment. "And she's like, 'We're going to Chinatown to get dumplings, eat them on a park bench, take the ferry to Ikea in Brooklyn.' She just wanted to explore everything," said Winston. In addition to her children and her partner, Rose is survived by her parents Carolyn and Jerry Friedman, her sisters Sophie and Nina and numerous admiring friends and colleagues. We will miss her wisdom, generosity, infectious humor and, above all, her voice. NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Morgan Hancock/Getty Images American rapper Macklemore will no longer be supporting Ed Sheeran ‘s Loop Tour amid a backlash against his “free Palestine” pleas. As the 4x Grammy winner took the stage for Sheeran’s tour earlier this month at MetLife Stadium, he called for “safety and peace” for all before performing his protest song “Hind’s Hall.” He later emphasized that his support for Palestinians is “in no way a criticism” of Jewish people. “To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters; criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, in no way is a criticism of you,” he said on stage. Related Stories News Princess Di Returns To 'SNL UK' As "Deeply Intelligent, Autonomous, Neurokinetic Android" In Cold Open Skewering King Charles, Ed Sheeran & AI News Ed Sheeran Admits To "Making Mistakes" With Macklemore, Calls Out "Systemic Injustice" In Gaza: "I'm So, So Sorry" In a statement, first shared with Rolling Stone, Messina Touring Group, promoter of the U.S. leg of Sheeran’s Loop Tour, said: “As the concert promoter for Ed Sheeran’s U.S. Loop Tour, we have been notified by venues on the upcoming U.S. tour dates that they will not allow a concert to take place with Macklemore on the lineup, which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans. After discussions with stakeholders, Macklemore will not be performing on the remaining support dates.” Watch on Deadline Macklemore posted a detailed response on Instagram, in which he reflected on difficult conversations with Sheeran and said his future on the tour was of no consequence when compared with the situation in Gaza. “I didn’t need 10 shows from Ed. I needed 2. Two chances to stand in front of 90,000 people and say the words that somehow became too dangerous to say. Free Palestine,” he wrote. “But if those words cost me the stage, while turning the conversation back to Palestine, then it was the most successful tour I’ve ever been on.” View this post on Instagram The decision followed the Israeli-American Council starting a petition urging Sheeran to “remove Macklemore” from the remainder of the tour. “This was an Ed Sheeran concert – not a political rally, not a protest, and not an activist event,” the petition reads. “The issue is not whether Macklemore has the right to hold political views.
